sections.html:
A single department handles valuing and billing. The Robeson County Tax Administrator holds both the assessor and collector roles. That covers listing and valuing real property, personal property and motor vehicles, collecting the tax, keeping land records and maps, and running reappraisals.

The office has three divisions. Assessment handles real property, reappraisal, personal property, individual and business listings, and motor vehicles. Collections has a customer service section and a delinquent collections section. Land Records and GIS keeps the maps and addresses.

The Lumberton office answers at 910-671-3060. The county's online tools let you look up real and personal property bills and search public land records. Before you search, gather the parcel number, the owner's name or a copy of the bill. Any one of them will pull up the record, and the parcel number is the fastest. A phone payment line (1-866-249-0705) also takes payments, and it carries a convenience fee.

sections.h2: When did Robeson County last reappraise?
sections.html:
The latest reappraisal took effect January 1, 2024. State law requires one at least every eight years, and the county commissioners have considered a four-year cycle so that fast-rising and slow-rising neighborhoods stay closer to market.

About 560 appraisal neighborhoods organize the work. Appraisers weigh cost, sales and income figures to produce a schedule of values, which the Board of Commissioners then adopts. Family sales, gifts, trades and deals between related companies are set aside as non-market transfers. A seller under pressure may also accept less than market value, so one sale price does not set an assessment.

Between reappraisals, your value moves only if something changes: new construction, demolition, remodeling, rezoning or a fix for a county error. Real property is listed permanently. You do not file a yearly listing unless you built, tore down a structure, or lost a program benefit.

Robeson mails real and personal property bills each August. They are due September 1, but interest does not start until after January 5. On January 6 a 2 percent charge applies, and the county adds three-fourths of a percent on the first of each month after that.

Robeson County real and personal property billing sequence
StepTiming
Bills mailedAugust
DueSeptember 1
Last day without interestJanuary 5
First interest charge2 percent, January 6
Added monthlyThree-fourths of 1 percent
Newspaper advertisingMarch, with a fee added to the bill

State law (G.S. 105-360) uses the same due date and interest steps. Once a bill is delinquent, collection can start with wage garnishment, bank attachment, foreclosure, income tax refund set-off or levies on rents.

sections.h2: Listing boats, mobile homes and business equipment
sections.html:
Personal property must be listed every year by January 31. Miss it and a 10 percent penalty is added. A written request postmarked by January 31 can win an extension to April 15.

  • Individual property: boats, motors, jet skis, mobile homes, aircraft and unlicensed vehicles such as trailers, campers and motorcycles.
  • Business property: machinery, equipment, computers, furniture, fixtures, supplies, farm machinery and race cars.
  • Anyone who owned these items on January 1 must list them.

If you listed last year, a form comes in the mail. If it doesn't, getting one is your job. Call 910-671-3060 and ask for extension 7320 or 7321 for individuals, or 7319 for business property.

Vehicle taxes ride along with the tag. Bills are mailed monthly, and each one is due at the start of the fourth month following a renewal or new tag. You then get 30 days of grace before 2 percent interest and the monthly three-fourths of a percent kick in.

An unpaid bill puts a state registration block on the vehicle, and the tag can't be renewed until you pay and the collector gives you a MAV-2 form. If you sell a vehicle and surrender the tag to the state, bring the bill of sale and the DMV receipt to the collector, because a refund or prorated bill may be due. A vehicle moved out of North Carolina needs the new state's registration card and the DMV surrender receipt. Keep these papers with your tax records until the collector confirms the account is closed.

Your appeal must be postmarked before the Board adjourns. That is usually late April, and the date is advertised ahead of the first meeting. Request the form in writing from the Tax Administrator at the Administration Center in Lumberton.

State law (G.S. 105-322) sets the board's first sitting between early April and early May. If you're still unhappy afterward, the next level is the state Property Tax Commission, and G.S. 105-290 allows 30 days from the mailed decision to give written notice.

Back your case with papers such as a purchase price or damage records. A recent closing statement, repair estimates or photos of problems the appraiser may not have seen all help. Check the date on your own notice, since the board's calendar is set and advertised each year. Keep a copy of everything you mail, and use a postmark you can prove.

The state offers three ways to cut a homeowner's bill, and you get to use just one of them. File Form AV-9 with the county assessor. January is the best month, though the office takes applications until June 1.

  • Elderly or disabled: the greater of $25,000 or 50 percent of a home's appraised value comes off. It applies to owners aged 65 or over, or with a permanent and total disability, under an income cap listed as $38,800 for 2026.
  • Disabled veteran: $45,000 of value is excluded, and neither age nor income matters. The county contact at 910-671-3071 helps with the NCDVA-9 certification.
  • Circuit breaker: the bill is limited to 4 percent of income at or below the cap and 5 percent between the cap and 150 percent of it ($58,200 for 2026). Anything above is deferred. You reapply yearly, and five years of ownership and residence come first.

Farm and forest land taxed at present use value is really a deferment. Take the land out of the program and the tax saved comes due, for the current year and three earlier ones, with interest. Property designated historic by local ordinance is taxed at half its appraised value.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed or due
sections.html:
The owner of record on January 1 is responsible for that year's tax. A June sale doesn't shift the bill off the seller. The buyer and seller normally divide the bill by agreement, but the invoice still goes to the seller.

Paying the collector directly at closing removes doubt. If the current bill isn't due yet, the office accepts a prepayment using the previous year's rate. Unpaid taxes on a house sold during the year can lead to both names being advertised.

The same office certifies your deed before recording, so one call can cover the balance and the certification. Ask for a written payoff figure, and keep it with your closing papers so the buyer's attorney can check it. For the current tax rate, call the office.

faqs.q: When does a Robeson County tax bill come due?
faqs.a: September 1 is the due date. You can pay through January 5 without interest, and 2 percent is added starting January 6.

faqs.q: When was the last Robeson County reappraisal?
faqs.a: It took effect January 1, 2024. The state minimum is every eight years, and commissioners have talked about a shorter four-year cycle.

faqs.q: Who owes the bill when a Robeson house sells in midyear?
faqs.a: Whoever owned it on January 1. The seller gets that year's bill, and closing papers usually prorate the cost.

faqs.q: How do older or disabled owners claim a Robeson County exclusion?
faqs.a: Submit Form AV-9 to the Tax Administration office, plus the NCDVA-9 certificate for a veteran claim. January is the target month, and June 1 is the last day accepted.

faqs.q: When must a Robeson County valuation appeal be filed?
faqs.a: Your appeal needs a postmark before the review board adjourns, usually in late April. Write to the Tax Administrator for the form.
